catalog_quote: Stress accent is quite noticeable in Salinan, and appears to be inherent in the roots and particles and inexplicable by any rules. Frequently, however, a word bears primary and secondary stress accents of nearly equal force which may be confused. Primary stress accent is denoted by an acute accent mark, secondary accent by a grave accent mark after the vowel thus stressed... Pitch accent is found, but is not of morphological significance; it is likewise inherent in certain syllables, generally of particles and grammatical elements. Thus the proclitic tarn, "then", and the enclitic ten, "again", generally bear an inflection of a slightly higher pitch... It appears to be more characteristic of the Migueleno dialect.

sources.citation: Turner, Katherine. 1987. Aspects of Salinan Grammar. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. xiii+240 pp. (eScholarship item 8483x855)
sources.quote: Stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive, supported by minimal pairs); in addition stress placement is grammatically exploited: 1st-person possessed nouns take first-syllable stress, 3rd-person possessed nouns take penultimate stress (with lengthening), and stress shift participates in denominal verb derivation. No default positional rule for unpossessed stems is given.
sources.locator: §1.3 Phonemes, pp. 39-40 ('Stress is phonemic.' appended to both the 20th-century and pre-contact phoneme charts); p. 42 minimal pairs for stress: té·lek 'my mouth' vs te·lék 'hole', ta·šáx 'my liver' vs ta·šax 'feathers', pá·talo? 'he danced' vs pa·tálo? 'he loosened it', ?éšxay 'rain' vs ?ešxáy 'dawn'; §2.2-2.21 pp. 69-71 ('pronominal possession is morphologically marked by placement of stress, affixation..'; 'The third person possessor is shown by penultimate stress'; 'For the first person possessed form the stress falls on the first syllable'); §§2.243-2.245 pp. 83-88 stress stays/shifts over two- and three-syllable stems; §2.111 p. 121 'Vowel lengthening in the stressed penultimate syllable of the third person possessed forms'; §4.712 p. ~150 'Stress shift. In verbs derived from non-body part nouns, stress seems to be a part of the derivational mechanism'.
sources.note: The standard modern grammar of Salinan (re-analysis of Mason + Harrington + Jacobsen records); states 'Stress is phonemic' with minimal pairs and documents morphological stress placement in possession -- should be added as a second source to a record that currently rests on Mason 1918 alone.
